title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
This is a model hallucination failure occurring at the point of legal document preparation. An AI legal tool called Irys generated fictitious case citations, non-existent quotes, and fabricated legal holdings, which were then included across multiple court filings. The failure reached the court because the lawyer using the tool believed it was performing citation verification when it was not, and no independent check confirmed the cases existed before filing.

The gap between what the tool was assumed to do and what it actually did is the proximate cause of the failure. A manual cite-check against an authoritative legal database before filing would have been sufficient to catch fabricated citations, since non-existent cases cannot be found in real legal repositories. The failure is not exotic, it is the known tendency of large language models to assert plausible-sounding but false information as fact, applied in a context where factual accuracy is legally required.

What is not established is whether the tool itself made any representation that it performed cite-checking, or whether that assumption originated entirely with the user. Admissions of error by counsel are not court findings of misconduct, and the case was reported as proceeding to trial.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers apologized after court filings in a Los Angeles lawsuit contained artificial intelligence-generated fake legal cases, non-existent quotes, and fabricated legal holdings. The homeowner, Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire left her Carson home uninhabitable, followed by water damage during repairs. She claimed State Farm delayed approving repairs, the work was never completed, and she and her husband subsequently lost their home to foreclosure after draining their savings and retirement accounts.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted using an AI tool called Irys to prepare motions, mistakenly believing it performed cite checks. She confirmed seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and quotes. Lead counsel Kenneth Katel accepted responsibility for the filings, and State Farm said it expects external counsel to meet high ethical standards. The case goes to trial in October. AI hallucinations are becoming increasingly common in legal work, with a database documenting 1,922 such cases worldwide, mostly in the United States.
